analysis.one_liner: Bans the sale and possession of semiautomatic assault weapons and ammunition magazines holding more than 10 rounds.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 89 cosponsors from both parties and held three days of hearings, but never left committee and never got a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have made it a federal crime to sell or own a semiautomatic assault weapon — naming Kalashnikov, Uzi, AR-15, and similar rifles — or a detachable magazine holding more than 10 rounds, though people who already owned them could keep them. It also would have let the Treasury Department add new weapons to the banned list, barred imports, added extra prison time for using one of these weapons in a violent or drug crime, and applied the same federal registration and transfer tax that machine guns face.
analysis.who_benefits: People living in communities affected by gun violence, and police who would face fewer of these weapons and high-capacity magazines on the street. Current owners were grandfathered in, so no one had to give up a gun they already lawfully owned.

how_it_helps.text: Makes it unlawful to transfer or possess semiautomatic assault weapons — expressly covering Kalashnikov, Uzi, Colt AR-15, Intratec TEC-9, and similar types — and any detachable magazine holding more than 10 rounds, while letting people keep ones they already lawfully owned.
Stops new imports of the covered weapons by removing the loophole that let semiautomatic versions of military-style rifles be brought in when fully automatic ones were banned.
Adds enhanced federal penalties for possessing or using one of these weapons during a crime of violence or drug trafficking crime, on top of the underlying offense.
Puts semiautomatic assault weapons under the same registration and transfer-tax system federal law already applies to machine guns, creating a paper trail for transfers of the grandfathered stock.

analysis.who_pays: Firearms manufacturers and importers lose the market for the named rifles and for magazines over 10 rounds, and dealers lose those sales. Future buyers lose access to the covered weapons, and current owners would face new registration requirements and transfer taxes on the guns they kept.

drawbacks.text: The grandfather clause is a major limit: every weapon and large-capacity magazine lawfully owned before the effective date stays legal forever, so the existing supply — the guns most likely to be resold on the street — remains in circulation.

The ban reaches common civilian firearms, not just military-style guns: it expressly covers the Ruger Mini 14, a standard semi-automatic rifle used for hunting and ranch work, and gives the Treasury Secretary standing authority to add more weapons to the list based on design features.

Current owners of covered weapons get no compensation or buyback; instead their guns become subject to federal registration and a transfer tax, so selling or inheriting one becomes a regulated, taxed transaction.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public-safety case is real — the bill targeted the specific rifles and high-capacity magazines used in mass shootings, and even a grandfathered ban would have stopped the future supply. But the design blunts its own effect: the grandfather clause leaves millions of covered weapons and magazines in circulation indefinitely, the magazine cutoff and feature lists draw bright lines that sweep in some ordinary rifles like the Mini 14 while missing functionally similar guns, and the registration-and-tax scheme would have been a real burden on the very current owners the bill lets keep their guns. An honest supporter would say this was a first step that traded immediate impact for political feasibility, and it never even got that far.

outcome.mechanism: It never left committee — after three days of subcommittee hearings in April 1989, neither the Judiciary nor the Ways and Means Committee ever brought it up for a vote, and it died when that Congress ended in January 1991.

narrative.text: Rep. Pete Stark introduced the bill on March 1, 1989, and it was referred jointly to the House Judiciary and Ways and Means Committees.
It was split between subcommittees — Trade under Ways and Means and Crime under Judiciary — and the Crime subcommittee held hearings on April 5, 6, and 10, 1989.
Support grew to 89 cosponsors, 83 Democrats and 6 Republicans, with more members adding on through May 1989.
After the hearings, no further action was ever taken: no committee vote, no report, no floor debate. The bill expired when the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Firearms manufacturers, importers, and dealers who kept selling the named rifles and large-capacity magazines, and buyers who wanted them, were better off because the bill never moved.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Gun makers and sellers of the banned weapons

for.name: Rep. Pete Stark
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited cosponsors; the bill text grew to carry 89 signatures.

for.name: 83 of 257 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, concentrated among California members after the January 1989 Stockton schoolyard shooting.

for.name: 6 of 175 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it small but real bipartisan support.

for.name: House Subcommittee on Crime
for.what_they_did: Held three days of hearings on the bill in April 1989.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Held subcommittee hearings in April 1989 but never reported the bill out or scheduled a committee vote; no floor action ever followed.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Sent the bill to its Trade subcommittee, where it sat without hearings or action for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: National Rifle Association
against.what_they_did: Fiercely opposed semiautomatic weapons bans in this era, pressuring members not to advance them.

sides.party_line_note: Support was heavily Democratic — 83 of 257 House Democrats signed on versus 6 of 175 Republicans — though the bill did attract a handful of Republican cosponsors.

industries.note: The bill would have outlawed the transfer and possession of their fastest-growing product line — semiautomatic versions of military-style rifles like the AK and AR-15 — and banned magazines over 10 rounds, cutting off future sales. The industry's interest in keeping those products on the market ran against the bill's public-safety purpose.

Dealers would have lost legal sales of the named weapons and high-capacity magazines after the 60-day effective date, and would have faced the federal registration system for transfers of grandfathered guns.
They could keep guns and magazines they already lawfully owned, but the weapons became subject to federal registration and transfer taxes, and resale outside the regulated system would be a crime.
